a: A worker who gets drunk
t: A drunken worker, or 'one who does this'?
p: The Hebrew of MS C reads 'One who does this', pointing back to the feasting of 18:32-33.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: a drunken worker
readings.plain: A worker who gets drunk

readings.w: Cairo Genizah MS C, an anthology of Ben Sira's sayings, folio V recto (transcription of Martin Abegg)
readings.en: one who does this
readings.plain: One who does this

why: The Plain translates the Greek, the base text of this site's Sirach. The Hebrew reads 'one who does this', which ties the verse to the warning against feasting on borrowed money in 18:32-33. The grandson, or the Hebrew copy he used, read or understood the line as a saying about drink.
b: This is one of the few places in chapters 19-23 where the Hebrew survives. David Kahana's edition (1912) prints only 19:1-2, 20:5-7, 20:13 and 21:22-23 from these chapters, all from MS C; the bensira.org transcriptions of MS C add 19:3, 20:22-23, 20:30-31, 21:26, 22:11-12, 22:21-22 and 23:11. MS C is a collection of excerpts, so its order is not the book's order. Everywhere else in these chapters the Greek is the oldest text there is.

a: glad at wickedness
t: Glad at heart or glad at wickedness?
p: Vaticanus says 'glad at heart', which makes joy itself a crime; the first hand of Sinaiticus has 'wickedness'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus as corrected
readings.en: rejoicing in heart
readings.plain: glad at heart

why: This is a departure from Swete's text. Vaticanus reads 'the one who rejoices in heart will be condemned', which would condemn simple gladness, though Ben Sira praises joy of heart elsewhere (30:22). The word kardia, 'heart', stands just before in 19:4 ('light in heart'), and a copyist's eye could easily carry it down. The first hand of Sinaiticus, the Latin and the text behind the KJV agree on 'wickedness', which fits the second half of the saying in 19:6.

a: for winter

Its sense is not certain: perhaps a man who borrows to build is like one who collects building stones in winter, when no one can build and the rains spoil the work, so his effort comes to nothing. The longer Greek gives a clearer picture, a man piling up stones for his own grave. The two Greek words, cheimōna and chōma, look alike, and one may have come from the other in copying. The Hebrew of this verse is lost.

readings.plain: but the wise keep their mouth in their heart

why: Vaticanus has no 'in' in the second line. Read as it stands, it says the wise speak what is in their heart, their words are their thoughts; with 'in', the wise keep their mouth in their heart and think before they speak. The Hebrew of MS C has 'in', and it may well be the original wording. The Plain follows the base text.

a: The lazy one is like a stone smeared with filth
t: Compared to a stone, or stoned?
p: Sinaiticus reads 'is stoned' for 'is compared', and so does the Latin.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: to a filthy stone the lazy one is compared
readings.plain: The lazy one is like a stone smeared with filth

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ), as reported in Swete's notes; the Latin ('In lapide luteo lapidatus est piger', Vulgate 22:1)
readings.en: is stoned (with a filthy stone)
readings.plain: The lazy one is pelted with a stone smeared with filth

why: 'Is compared', synneblēthē, is the reading of Vaticanus and Alexandrinus and is repeated in 22:2. Sinaiticus's 'is stoned', elithobolēthē, sounds alike and makes a lively picture; the Latin has it in both verses ('the lazy one is stoned with a muddy stone ... with the dung of oxen'), and the Douay-Rheims follows the Latin.

a: will inherit a husband
t: Inherit a husband, or be her husband's inheritance?
p: The Greek says she 'will inherit her husband'; the longer Greek, the Latin and the KJV read differently.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: will inherit her husband
readings.plain: will inherit a husband

readings.w: Codex 248, a minuscule of the longer Greek text, as printed by Hart (1909)
readings.en: will inherit from her husband
readings.plain: will receive an inheritance from her husband

readings.w: The Latin ('Filia prudens hæreditas viro suo', Vulgate 22:4); KJV ('shall bring an inheritance to her husband')
readings.en: is an inheritance for her husband
readings.plain: will be an inheritance for her husband

why: 'Will inherit her husband' most likely means she will gain one, as land is gained by inheritance. Codex 248's genitive, 'from her husband', makes her an heir of his property. The Latin and the KJV turn it around: a sensible daughter is a treasure for the man she marries. All three see her good sense as a gain; they differ on who gains.

why: As at 19:18: the lines are not in Vaticanus, Sinaiticus or Alexandrinus as Swete reports them, nor in the Clementine Vulgate. The Plain translates them from Hart's codex 248, which has them after 22:6, as the KJV does. They go with 22:3-5 on children who shame or honor their families. This verse and the next go together.

a: Stakes
p: Alexandrinus and Ephraemi have 'pebbles' (chalikes) for 'stakes' (charakes).

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: stakes, a fence of stakes
readings.plain: Stakes

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD) and Codex Ephraemi (C), as reported in Swete's notes; also noted in the margin of Hart's codex 248
readings.en: pebbles, small stones
readings.plain: Pebbles

why: The two Greek words differ by one letter. Stakes set on a hill, a fence or a row of vineyard poles, fit 'will not hold out against the wind'. The Latin has both: pali in excelsis, et cæmenta sine impensa posita, 'stakes on high places, and stonework laid without cost' (Vulgate 22:21).

a: If you draw a sword against a friend,
p: The Hebrew of MS C is a command: 'Do not draw a sword against a friend ... for there is atonement'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: against a friend if you draw a sword
readings.plain: If you draw a sword against a friend,

readings.w: Cairo Genizah MS C, an anthology of Ben Sira's sayings, folio VI verso (transcription of Shulamit Elizur)
readings.en: do not draw a sword
readings.plain: Do not draw a sword against a friend;

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew forbids drawing a sword and then comforts the offender: 'do not fear, for there is atonement' (kofer, a ransom or settlement). The Greek assumes the quarrel has happened and promises 'a way back'. Either way, a quarrel can be mended; betrayal cannot (22:22).

a: If you open your mouth against a friend,
p: The Hebrew of MS C says 'Do not open your mouth against a friend; do not worry, for there is repentance'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: against a friend if you open your mouth
readings.plain: If you open your mouth against a friend,

readings.w: Cairo Genizah MS C, an anthology of Ben Sira's sayings, folio VI verso
readings.en: do not open your mouth
readings.plain: Do not open your mouth against a friend;

why: As at 22:21, the Hebrew forbids and the Greek supposes. The Hebrew's reason is teshuvah, 'return, repentance'; the Greek has diallagē, 'reconciliation'. MS C stops after this line, so the list of what ends a friendship survives only in Greek.

readings.plain: you can be filled together with him

readings.en: you may rejoice
readings.plain: you can rejoice with him

why: The Plain keeps Vaticanus. 'Filled' suggests sharing a friend's good things at his table; 'rejoice' is the easier word.

a: Master of my life
p: Alexandrinus reads 'Father and God of my life', the same words as 23:4.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: Master of my life
readings.plain: Master of my life

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A), as reported in Swete's notes
readings.en: God of my life
readings.plain: God of my life

readings.w: Codex 248, a minuscule of the longer Greek text, as printed by Hart (1909)
readings.en: Master of all life
readings.plain: Master of all life

why: Vaticanus has 'Master' here and 'God' in 23:4, so the two addresses differ. Alexandrinus makes them the same. Codex 248 has 'Master of all life', and the KJV paraphrases: 'Father and Governor of all my whole life'.

readings.en: and my enemy will rejoice over me
readings.plain: while my enemy gloats over me

readings.w: Codex 248, a minuscule of the longer Greek text, as printed by Hart (1909); KJV ('and my sins abound to my destruction ... and mine enemy rejoice over me, whose hope is far from thy mercy')

why: Codex 248 also adds 'to destruction' (eis syntribēn) after 'my sins will not pile up', and in 23:2 reads 'you, Lord, will not spare' and 'do not let the insults of sinners pass'. None of this is in Vaticanus.

a: the Holy One
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus read 'the Most High'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: of the Holy One
readings.plain: the Holy One

readings.en: of the Most High
readings.plain: the Most High

why: 'The Holy One' stands in Vaticanus and in codex 248. Both are titles of God that a pious speaker might use to avoid the divine name; the KJV renders 'the Holy One'.

a: names the Name
p: Vaticanus says only 'names'; Alexandrinus and a corrector of Sinaiticus add 'the name of the Lord'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: naming
readings.plain: names the Name

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus as corrected (ℵc.a) and Codex Alexandrinus (A), as reported in Swete's notes; KJV ('nameth God')
readings.orig: ὀνομάζων διὰ παντὸς τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου
readings.en: naming the name of the Lord continually
readings.plain: names the name of the Lord

why: In Vaticanus the verb has no object, but 23:9 ('naming the Holy One') shows what is meant, so the Plain writes 'the Name', the reverent Jewish way to refer to God's name (as in Leviticus 24:16). The other codices spell it out.

a: when you take your seat among the great
p: Vaticanus's first hand reads 'he sits'; a corrector, Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus read 'you sit' or 'you will sit'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus as corrected (Bc) and Codex Alexandrinus (A); Codex Sinaiticus has 'you will sit'; Codex 248, a minuscule of the longer Greek text, as printed by Hart (1909) ('you will sit'); KJV
readings.en: you sit in council
readings.plain: when you take your seat among the great

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete (first hand)
readings.en: he sits in council
readings.plain: for he sits in council among the great

why: This is a departure from Swete's text, which prints the first hand of Vaticanus, synedreuei, 'he sits'. That reading gives no clear subject. The second person, 'you sit', is read by a corrector of Vaticanus and by Alexandrinus, and the future 'you will sit' by Sinaiticus and codex 248. It fits the rest of the verse, which speaks to 'you'. The difference is one letter.

readings.plain: paying attention to the Lord's commandments.

readings.w: Codex 248, a minuscule of the longer Greek text, as printed by Hart (1909); KJV 23:28 ('It is great glory to follow the Lord, and to be received of him is long life')
readings.orig: τοῦ προσέχοντος ἐντολαῖς θεοῦ. δόξα μεγάλη ἀκολουθεῖν θεῷ, μακρότης δὲ ἡμερῶν τὸ προσληφθῆναί σε ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ.
